places.name: 京都中華 ハマムラ 府庁前店 (Kyoto Chuka Hamamura (Fuchomae))
places.neighborhood: Nakagyo-ku, across from the Kyoto Prefectural Office (Fuchom
places.cuisine: Kyoto-style Chinese

noodles.notes: Thin straight noodles served under a thick ankake (starch-bound) sauce rather than in a loose soup; one source notes the noodles are seared on one side before the sauce is ladled over them.

ramen.signature_bowl: Karashi soba (からしそば) — thin straight noodles bound in a light, glossy ankake sauce over chicken-and-kombu stock, loaded with pork and vegetables and finished with a fierce sheet of hot Japanese mustard (karashi). A Kyoto-Chinese specialty served as a dinner item; an evening-only offering at this location.
ramen.chashu: No braised or grilled chashu in the ramen sense; the protein is sliced pork simmered into the ankake topping alongside the vegetables.

gf.note: Wheat noodles plus a soy-based, starch-thickened ankake sauce; nothing rice- or konjac-noodle and no GF tare is documented. Not celiac-safe.

vegan.note: The signature bowl is built on chicken-gara stock with sliced pork in the ankake; no documented kombu/shiitake plant-only broth bowl. The kitchen does run a vegetable-forward, oil-controlled style, so a modified veg dish could be worth asking about, but nothing vegan is confirmed.

ramen.pantheon: This is Kyoto-Chinese, not gotochi ramen: a house that has cooked the genteel, oil-restrained Chinese of the old geisha quarters since 1924, where chicken and kombu do the work that garlic and lard do elsewhere. Its karashi soba is the soul of that lineage — a delicate, almost dashi-clear ankake draped over thin noodles, then jolted awake by a roaring hit of hot mustard, refinement and shock in one bowl.

places.name: ラーメン また此処で (Ramen Mata Koko de)
places.neighborhood: Nishi-Shichijo / Nishioji-Shichijo, Shimogyo-ku (near JR Nis
places.cuisine: Jiro-style ramen

noodles.notes: Extra-thick, wavy self-made noodles with a strong wheat aroma and substantial chew; ~300g in the regular size. Slurpable rather than punishingly firm despite the bulk.

ramen.signature_bowl: Ramen (並ラーメン) - 300g of thick wavy noodles in an emulsified sweet pork-bone shoyu broth, crowned with the Jiro mountain of bean sprouts and cabbage, back-fat (seabura), and grated garlic. Call your toppings at the counter (mashi for extra veg/fat/garlic). A tsukemen version is also offered.
ramen.chashu: Thick, melt-in-the-mouth braised pork (buta), served 2 slices standard with a 5-slice option; tender, gelatinous edges in the Jiro tradition.

gf.note: Jiro-style bowls are built on wheat: thick wheat-and-kansui noodles and a wheat-based shoyu tare over a pork broth. No rice/konjac noodle or GF option is documented. Not celiac-safe.

vegan.note: Core of the bowl is a pork-bone (tonkotsu) broth with pork back-fat and braised pork; shoyu tare and pork are pervasive. No plant-based broth option is documented.

ramen.pantheon: A faithful piece of the Ramen Jiro universe transplanted to Kyoto by a chef who spent over a decade in a celebrated Jiro-style kitchen: a sweet, emulsified pork-bone soup buried under a mountain of bean sprouts, cabbage, back-fat and garlic. What sets it apart is a distinctly Kyoto restraint in the shoyu seasoning, dialing back the usual Jiro saltiness so the broth's natural pork sweetness leads.

places.name: あぶらそば 油珉 (Abura Soba Yumin)
places.neighborhood: 百万遍・田中門前町（左京区、京大近く） / Hyakumanben, Sakyo-ku, near Kyoto Univ
places.cuisine: Abura-soba (brothless oil noodles)

noodles.notes: House-made noodles from 100% domestic wheat, mochi-mochi chewy with a springy bite. The standard abura soba and spicy version share a common house noodle; the back-fat vegetable bowl uses a separate extra-thick, wavy, jiro-style noodle with a wari-wari chew. Base portion around 180g, scalable up to roughly 540g.

ramen.signature_bowl: 背脂ヤサイあぶらそば (Se-abura Yasai Abura Soba) — the brothless back-fat vegetable bowl on the thick jiro-style noodle; the shoyu-leaning standard あぶらそば is the lighter all-rounder.
ramen.chashu: A single thick-cut slab of tender braised pork chashu tops the signature vegetable bowl.

gf.note: Brothless abura soba built on wheat-and-kansui house noodles with a shoyu-forward (wheat) tare; no rice or konjac noodle option is documented. Not celiac-safe.

vegan.note: Bowls are dressed with pork back fat, braised pork chashu and a savory shoyu tare; no documented plant-only build. The vegetable variant still rides on back fat and meat, so it is not vegan.

ramen.pantheon: A brothless Kyoto abura soba where the soul lives in the tare-slicked noodle rather than a soup: a shoyu-forward sauce with a faintly creamy sweetness, finished tableside with vinegar, garlic and chili oil. Its flagship leans into the city's back-fat heritage and a jiro-style mountain of cabbage, sprouts and lard on a thick wavy noodle — a "soupless Jiro shio" you mix, not sip.

places.name: 台湾まぜそば専門店 脳天喜。 (Taiwan Mazesoba Senmonten Noutenki (Kyoto Me)
places.neighborhood: Kamigyō-ku, Senbon-Demizu (Nijō Stn / northwest of Nijō Castle)
places.cuisine: Taiwanese mazesoba

noodles.notes: Two noodle choices: a chunky medium-thick noodle blending whole-grain and wheat flour, or a rippled "wing" noodle (from a renowned Kyoto noodle maker) whose wavy surface grips the spicy mince and sauce. The wing noodle is the popular pick for how well the ingredients cling.

ramen.signature_bowl: Tonporo Taiwan Mazesoba (東坡肉台湾まぜそば) — brothless mixed noodles with spicy Taiwan mince, crowned with a slab of melting braised pork belly. Mix everything, then finish with a rice ball (追い飯) dunked into the leftover sauce.
ramen.chashu: The heart is not a typical ramen chashu but Chinese-style 東坡肉 (Dongpo/tonporo) braised pork belly — slow-cooked by a Chinese chef until quivering-tender, sweet-savory, with the star anise kept gentle for the Japanese palate. A diced-pork rice bowl and ajitama-chashu version are also offered.
notable_toppings: 10 table condiments incl. Aomori garlic-vinegar and niboshi-vinegar

gf.note: Both noodle options are wheat-based (whole-grain/wheat blend and wing noodle), the Taiwan mince and tare carry soy/wheat seasoning, and the rice finisher shares the same sauce. No gluten-free noodle or tare is documented.

vegan.note: Core dish is built on pork mince, braised pork belly, raw egg yolk and fish powder; the side ramen is chicken paitan. No documented plant-based broth or topping set.

ramen.pantheon: A Kyoto temple to Nagoya-born Taiwan mazesoba — the brothless, garlic-and-chili mince bowl you toss together yourself — but with a twist: a Chinese chef tops it with quivering Dongpo braised pork belly instead of the usual char siu. Choose your noodle, mix in the raw yolk, then dunk a rice ball into the lingering spicy-savory sauce for the classic two-act finish.

places.name: 力餅食堂 柿仲 (Chikara Mochi Shokudo Kakichu)
places.neighborhood: Fushimi-ku, Fukakusa shopping street (JR Fujinomori / Keihan Fukakusa Stn)
places.cuisine: Machi-chūka chuka-soba (neighborhood Chinese noodles)

noodles.notes: Thin, straight noodles that slide smoothly and easily into the mouth — light and unfussy, matched to the delicate broth rather than a chewy modern ramen noodle.

ramen.signature_bowl: 中華そば (chuka soba) — the house bowl: a pale, gentle light-shoyu soup with thin straight noodles, served the old-shokudo way for under 1000 yen.
ramen.chashu: Sliced braised pork chashu, cut surprisingly thick for such a light bowl — a homely, tender slice rather than an aburi/char-grilled or melt-and-collapse style.

gf.note: Standard wheat-and-kansui chuka noodles in a soy-sauce (wheat) broth; this is a traditional town shokudo with no documented rice- or konjac-noodle or gluten-free tare option.

vegan.note: The bowl is built on an animal/dashi base, soy tare, fish-cake kamaboko and pork chashu; no plant-broth (kombu/shiitake/veg) version is documented.

ramen.pantheon: This is chuka soba in its most nostalgic, home-cooked form: the kind of pale, gentle light-shoyu bowl an old Kyoto neighborhood eatery has ladled out for generations, closer in spirit to a clear udon-soba broth than to any modern ramen specialist. Its soul is restraint — a clean, kind soup you could eat every day without tiring of it, dressed with two slices of kamaboko, menma and bright Kujo negi.

places.name: 中華そば 六 (Chuka Soba Roku)
places.neighborhood: 河原町四条（GOOD NATURE STATION 2F）
places.cuisine: Duck-broth chuka-soba

noodles.notes: Thin, straight custom-made noodles with a firm bite, chosen to define against the silky clear broth.

ramen.signature_bowl: Chuka soba (中華そば) — a crystal-clear duck-forward chukasoba built on a five-bone stock; optionally finished with the table-side trio of pork-and-water-chestnut wontons.
ramen.chashu: Pork chashu cooked low in a convection oven to stay moist and juicy rather than braised soft, served refined and clean to match the delicate soup.
notable_toppings: side wontons (pork, onion, water chestnut, celery)

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui noodles and a shoyu-style tare; no rice/konjac noodle or gluten-free seasoning is documented. Not celiac-safe.

vegan.note: Broth is drawn from duck, chicken, venison, beef and pork bones with animal-fat finishing oil and pork chashu; no plant-only bowl is offered.

ramen.pantheon: A chef-driven, modern-original take on chukasoba: instead of one signature bone, the soup is a layered consommé pulled from duck, chicken, venison, beef and pork and rounded with porcini, dried shiitake, tomato and longan, so you taste depth without weight. It reads less like a regional gotochi ramen and more like a refined-Chinese-kitchen interpretation of the clear-soup Kyoto bowl, where finesse and aromatics carry the lineage.

places.name: 中華 六六 (Chuka Rokuroku)
places.neighborhood: Kita-ku, Kitaōji / Horikawa-Kitaōji (Murasakino)
places.cuisine: Machi-chūka (neighborhood Chinese) / chuka-soba

noodles.notes: Medium-thick, straight, translucent noodles of the old-school machi-chuka type — soft and not the focus of the bowl; the soup and toppings carry it.

ramen.signature_bowl: Chuka soba (中華そば) — the house clear soy-sauce noodle bowl
ramen.chashu: A thick, single cut of braised pork chashu with a notably good lean-to-fat balance.

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui noodles plus a soy-sauce (wheat) tare in a townhouse Chinese kitchen with no documented rice/konjac-noodle or GF option — not celiac-safe.

vegan.note: A meat-stock soy-sauce broth with pork chashu and no documented plant-based bowl; not vegan.

ramen.pantheon: This is a town-Chinese chuka soba rather than a specialist's ramen: a clear, gently sweet soy-sauce soup whose soul is the perfume of scallion and the mellow sweetness of slow-cooked onion, served the old machiya way. It leans nostalgic and homey — light and easy-drinking, defined more by its tender housemade-style menma and a generous slab of chashu than by any regional ramen lineage.

places.name: キラメキノトリ (Kirameki no Tori)
places.neighborhood: Kamigyo-ku, Demizu-cho — west of the Kyoto Imperial Palace (
places.cuisine: Chicken paitan ramen

noodles.notes: House-made noodles from the group's own noodle factory using 100% Hokkaido wheat; medium-thick straight cut with a chewy, mochi-mochi bite that clings to the creamy broth.

ramen.signature_bowl: Tori paitan ramen, shio version (the salt tare best showcases the chicken umami, finished with lemon); the night-only Taiwan mazesoba is the other house specialty.
ramen.chashu: Chicken thigh chashu — tender and moist, served with a seared skin for a bit of char and bite (no pork in the signature bowl).

gf.note: Noodles are wheat (100% Hokkaido wheat) plus kansui, and the shoyu/miso tare add wheat; no rice- or konjac-noodle or GF option is documented. Not celiac-safe.

vegan.note: The soul of the bowl is a long-simmered chicken paitan with chicken chashu and chicken fat; no plant-based broth or vegan bowl is documented.

ramen.pantheon: A modern tori-paitan specialist whose soul is a creamy, deeply emulsified chicken broth simmered to a milky richness yet finished clean enough to drink to the bottom. Order it shio with a squeeze of lemon and you taste the lineage of the contemporary chicken-paitan movement rather than any one regional tradition — pure poultry umami carried by chewy Hokkaido-wheat noodles and a skin-seared chicken chashu.

places.name: 御旅飯店 (Otabi Hanten)
places.neighborhood: Kamigyō-ku, Kitaōji-Ōmiya (Funaokayama / in front of Daitoku-ji; Kuramaguchi Subway Stn)
places.cuisine: Machi-chūka (neighborhood Chinese) / chuka-soba

noodles.notes: Standard old-school 中華そば noodles in the neighborhood-Chinese idiom; specific gauge, shape and hydration are not documented.

ramen.signature_bowl: 中華そば (the house Chinese soba) — a chicken-bone shoyu bowl; note the shop's true headliner is actually the 御旅丼 rice bowl, with the noodle dishes a beloved sideline. Also offered as a mini-ramen add-on (+¥200) to a rice set.

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui noodles and a wheat-based soy tare; no rice/konjac-noodle or gluten-free option is documented at this neighborhood Chinese diner. Not celiac-safe.

vegan.note: The bowl is built on a chicken-bone broth with a soy tare; no plant-based (kombu/shiitake/vegetable) broth option is documented. Not vegan.

ramen.pantheon: An everyday Kyoto 町中華 (neighborhood Chinese) bowl rather than a destination ramen: a clear chicken-bone shoyu soup, seasoned bold and on the stronger side, in the homey Showa-era 中華そば tradition you find in the back-streets near Funaokayama and Daitoku-ji. You taste the lineage of the all-purpose Chinese kitchen — the same stock that anchors its famous rice bowls — rather than a single regional school.

places.name: いいちょ ラーメン (Iicho Ramen)
places.neighborhood: Shimogamo, Sakyō-ku (Kitaōji Subway Stn / Shimogamo)
places.cuisine: Light shoyu chuka-soba

noodles.notes: Thin, straight noodles from a local Kyoto noodle maker, with a slightly soft, traditional mid-century bite (細めのストレート). Made by an outside noodle factory, not in-house.

ramen.signature_bowl: Shoyu chuka soba (醤油ラーメン) — the chicken-and-pork blended soy-sauce bowl; add chashu for the chashu-men, and pair with the shop's signature fried rice (yakimeshi) as a set.
ramen.chashu: Thin-sliced pork chashu braised for about half a day in the shop's own Sawai soy-sauce tare before serving (薄切りチャーシュー).

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui noodles plus a wheat-based soy-sauce (shoyu) tare; no rice/konjac noodle or gluten-free tare option is documented. Not celiac-safe.

vegan.note: Broth is built on chicken and pork bones with a soy tare and pork back-fat, and chashu tops the bowl. No plant-based broth option is documented.

ramen.pantheon: A traditional Kyoto-style soy bowl that carries the lineage of the long-gone Iwakura ramen: a chicken-and-pork blend simmered to a faintly clouded, deeply chicken-scented broth, seasoned with a punchy artisanal Kyoto soy sauce and finished with melting back-fat. You taste the old Rakuhoku neighborhoods in every sip — comfort-food shoyu rather than flashy modern ramen.

places.name: 麺屋 誉 (Menya Homare)
places.neighborhood: Fukakusa, Fushimi-ku (around Fujinomori Stn)
places.cuisine: Rich tonkotsu-shoyu ramen / mazesoba

noodles.notes: Custom noodles from the venerable Kyoto maker Teigaku (棣鄂), founded 1931 — medium-thick, mostly straight with a very subtle wave, cut slightly thinner than typical Hakata noodles. Springy, chewy and built for slurping, with enough body to stand up to the heavy soup. Firmness is adjustable to order.

ramen.signature_bowl: 特製濃厚豚骨醤油ラーメン (Tokusei rich tonkotsu-shoyu ramen) — the deluxe bowl loaded with both chashu styles, an ajitama, greens and nori.
ramen.chashu: A two-style pairing: smoky low-temperature braised pork with deep savory richness, plus a pastrami-style cured loin crowned with cracked black pepper — both cooked sous-vide-tender.

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui noodles plus a soy-sauce (wheat) tare over a pork-and-chicken broth; no rice- or konjac-noodle or gluten-free tare option is documented. Not celiac-safe.

vegan.note: The soul of the bowl is a long-simmered pork-bone and chicken broth dressed with shoyu tare, pork back-fat/chicken oil and pork chashu — animal-derived throughout. No plant-based broth bowl is documented.

ramen.pantheon: A thick, velvety pork-and-chicken paitan lacquered with a bold soy tare — this bowl leans into the Yokohama Iekei spirit of muscular tonkotsu-shoyu, but pushes the richness and salt-forward punch harder than Kyoto's gentler local style. You taste the deep, faintly sweet collagen of slow-rendered pork bones, sharpened by a generous soy backbone and a table-side hit of grated garlic and niboshi vinegar.

places.name: 和麺ぐり虎 京都本店 (Wamen Guriko Kyoto Honten)
places.neighborhood: Nakagyō-ku, Rokkaku-dōri Higashinotōin (Karasuma-Oike / Shijō-Karasuma)
places.cuisine: Chicken-shio & sea-bream-shio ramen / tsukemen / mazesoba

noodles.notes: Special noodle of 100% domestic wheat; medium-thin straight cut renewed in April 2025 to be slightly thicker for a more satisfying bite. Notable for a pronounced wheat aroma, supple texture, firm clean bite and smooth throat-feel.

ramen.signature_bowl: Tori-shio ramen (chicken-salt) — the house signature; also celebrated for the tai-shio ramen made with whole domestic wild red sea bream. Order the 特製 (special) version to get the full topping set.
ramen.chashu: Low-temperature-style braised pork chashu, moist and tender, releasing more meat umami the longer you chew.

gf.note: Wheat noodles are 100% domestic wheat plus kansui, and the dashi/tare layer in bonito (katsuo) and other umami — not celiac-safe. No rice or konjac noodle option is documented.

vegan.note: Broths are built on chicken, sea bream, clam/shellfish dashi, and bonito flakes, with pork chashu — no documented plant-based bowl. The shiitake/kombu in the tare sit atop animal stocks, not a standalone vegan broth.

ramen.pantheon: A polished modern-Japanese kaiseki take on shio ramen, where the soul lives in a crystal-clear chicken broth deepened with delicate clam dashi — or, in the sister bowl, the sweet umami of whole wild red sea bream. The salt tare, aged with Okinawa and Niigata sea salts plus kombu, shiitake and bonito, gives a soft, refined salinity that tastes unmistakably of careful Japanese dashi craft rather than any single regional lineage.

places.name: 麺や 鳥の鶏次 KYOTO 四条河原町店 (Men-ya Tori no Keiji KYOTO Shijo Kawaramachi)
places.neighborhood: Shimogyō-ku / Kyoto-Kawaramachi Stn, Shijō-Kawaramachi
places.cuisine: Chicken paitan (creamy chicken broth)

noodles.notes: Smooth, slightly flat medium-thick noodles with good elasticity and strong broth pickup; sources vary between straight and gently wavy. Built to carry the aerated, creamy chicken broth.

ramen.signature_bowl: 鶏そば (塩) — chicken shio paitan, the core bowl that best showcases the pure chicken broth. Flavored variations include 鶏次レッド (chili oil), 鶏次ブラック (black-garlic mayu), 鶏次グリーン (matcha), 鶏そばフロマージュ (cheese), and トリュフそば (truffle).
ramen.chashu: Two kinds of house-made low-temperature chicken rare chashu — tender, juicy, odor-free thigh and breast; mild-flavored so it complements rather than competes with the broth.

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui noodles plus a shoyu-tare option mean these bowls are not celiac-safe. No rice/konjac-noodle or GF-tare option is documented.

vegan.note: The entire identity is chicken: broth is domestic chicken and water only, tare and chashu are chicken-based, so all bowls are animal-derived. No plant-broth option is offered (the shop is notably popular with Muslim diners precisely because everything is chicken, not pork).

ramen.pantheon: A foam-style tori paitan in the modern Osaka lineage — fresh domestic chicken and water simmered over eight hours, then blitzed tableside-fresh into an aerated, cappuccino-like froth so creamy and sweet it tastes almost dairy-rich, with no vegetables or seafood to dilute the pure poultry soul. The shio reads cleanest, while playful black-garlic, chili-oil, matcha, cheese and truffle riffs push the genre into dessert-like indulgence.

places.name: ぎょうざ処 高辻 亮昌 本店 (Gyoza-dokoro Takatsuji Sukemasa Honten)
places.neighborhood: Shimogyo Ward, Takatsuji / near Shijo Karasuma, Karasuma Stn
places.cuisine: Neighborhood Chinese & gyoza

places.name: 中華料理 大鵬 (Chuka Ryori Taiho)
places.neighborhood: 中京区 西ノ京 / 二条駅すぐ (Nishinokyo, near JR Nijo Station)
places.cuisine: Town-Chinese / Sichuan

noodles.notes: The dry tantanmen rides on thin, non-kansui straight noodles (described as Kagawa-style fine udon) rather than typical kansui ramen noodles, chosen to soak up the sesame-chili sauce pooled at the bottom of the bowl. Toss top-to-bottom before eating. Thickness/shape for the soup tantanmen is not separately documented.

ramen.signature_bowl: Tantanmen — order the shiru-nashi (dry) tantanmen for the house's most distinctive bowl; a soup tantanmen is also offered. (Note: this is a Sichuan town-Chinese kitchen whose true icons are teridon and Omi-beef mapo tofu, with tantanmen as its standout noodle dish.)

gf.note: Wheat noodles throughout (the dry tantanmen uses non-kansui wheat udon-style noodles) plus a soy/sesame-based Sichuan sauce; no rice-noodle or gluten-free option is documented. Not celiac-safe.

vegan.note: The tantanmen is built on minced pork and a dashi-backed broth, and the kitchen's repertoire leans heavily on pork, Omi beef and chicken. No documented plant-broth, meat-free bowl.

ramen.pantheon: This is no ramen-counter bowl but a Sichuan kitchen's tantanmen: a sesame-rich, faintly sweet broth wired tight with dashi and a whisper of vinegar, then lit up by sweat-coaxing mala heat and the citrus-numbing perfume of huajiao. The prized dry version pools that chili-sesame sauce beneath slick thin noodles, peanuts and minced pork — closer to Chengdu's street dandan than to any Japanese gotochi lineage.

places.name: 京都和麺 諭吉本舗 (Kyoto Wamen Yukichi Honpo)
places.neighborhood: Nakagyō-ku, Teramachi-dōri Takoyakushi (~3 min walk from Kyoto-Kawaramachi Stn)
places.cuisine: Japanese-style (wafū) chuka-soba

noodles.notes: Self-made noodles cut fresh daily, with a choice of thin, thick, or hand-kneaded (te-momi) styles matched to the soup; the thin straight cut is the default for the wafu chuka soba.

ramen.signature_bowl: Wamen (和麺) — the wafu chuka soba built on a chicken-and-shellfish dashi; premium versions crown it with a seared A5 wagyu steak finished tableside and a wash of truffle oil.
ramen.chashu: On the premium bowls the headline protein is seared A5 wagyu steak rather than traditional braised pork; the standard chuka soba's pork chashu is not clearly documented.

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui ramen noodles plus a shoyu-leaning tare make this unsafe for celiacs; no rice or konjac noodle option is documented.

vegan.note: The broth is built on chicken bones blended with clam/shellfish dashi, and bowls feature egg and wagyu, so there is no plant-based option.

ramen.pantheon: A modern Kyoto wafu original rather than a regional throwback: its soul is a delicate double soup of chicken-gara cut with clam-and-shellfish dashi, seasoned light with shio and shoyu so the marine umami stays clear and elegant. The shop then gilds that restrained Japanese base with luxury flourishes — a tableside-seared A5 wagyu steak and a perfume of truffle oil — pushing the bowl toward a near-French extravagance.

trading_verified.why: The operator's own 店舗情報 page still lists 「京都和麺 諭吉本舗 / 京都府京都市中京区寺町通蛸薬師上る東側町506−1 / 営業時間 11:30～15:00 17:00～21:30」, matching the record's address. places.name: 麺屋 坂本 (Menya Sakamoto)
places.neighborhood: Kita-ku, Kuramaguchi Stn
places.cuisine: Tsukemen & ramen

noodles.notes: Noodles sourced from the famed Tokyo mill Asakusa Kaika-ro (浅草開化楼) — rarely seen in Kansai — slightly flat, chewy straight noodles with substantial bite, chosen to carry the delicate clear broth.

ramen.signature_bowl: Tori Chuka Soba (鶏中華そば) — clear chicken-and-seafood shoyu ramen; also celebrated for the chilled shio soba (塩冷やしそば) in warmer months, finished with sudachi citrus.
ramen.chashu: Braised pork chashu served in the Tokyo style; specific cut (loin vs belly) not documented.

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui ramen noodles plus a wheat-based shoyu tare; no rice-noodle or gluten-free option is documented.

vegan.note: Broth is built on chicken plus fish dashi (niboshi, katsuo/saba-bushi, kombu) with pork chashu; no documented plant-based broth or topping set.

ramen.pantheon: A clean-soup (chintan) shop in the refined Tokyo tradition: a base of whole heritage chickens (momiji-dori, sakura-dori) layered with niboshi, bonito, mackerel flakes and Rausu kombu, then a slightly sweet shoyu kaeshi or a month-aged shio tare. You taste the lineage in the clarity — the chilled shio version is praised as elegant enough to recall a kaiseki broth, a delicate counterpoint to Kyoto's heavier se-abura tradition.

places.name: びし屋 (Bishiya)
places.neighborhood: Sakyō-ku, Ichijōji (Eizan Railway Ichijōji Stn)
places.cuisine: Tsukemen & ramen

noodles.notes: In-house noodles milled from Hokkaido domestic wheat; thick, straight (near hira-uchi/flat) for the tsukemen with strong wheat fragrance and a chewy, elastic bite that stands up to the thick broth. The ramen uses a slightly slimmer medium-thick straight noodle. Tsukemen portions chosen 200-300g.

ramen.signature_bowl: Tonkotsu-shoyu ramen — the house bowl — or the pork-bone-and-seafood (tonkotsu-gyokai) tsukemen with thick handmade noodles and yuzu-dashi finishing rice.
ramen.chashu: Generous thick-cut braised pork slices, soft and tender with notably high-quality, well-rendered fat; four substantial pieces in a typical bowl.

gf.note: Wheat noodles are milled in-house from domestic wheat, and the broth is a pork/seafood/chicken stock with a soy (wheat-based) tare. No rice- or konjac-noodle or gluten-free option is documented; not celiac-safe.

vegan.note: Broth is built on pork bone, chicken bones and fish/seafood dashi, topped with pork chashu. No plant-based broth bowl is documented.

ramen.pantheon: In the dense ramen corridor of Ichijoji, this is a thick, concentrated pork-bone-and-soy bowl whose soul is a deeply rendered tonkotsu rounded out with chicken and a clear current of seafood umami — rich and faintly sweet, yet scrubbed of any barnyard pork funk. Though its thick straight noodles, spinach and nori echo the look of Yokohama iekei, the kitchen pushes its own modern blend: a sharper soy edge, a gyokai sweetness, and a thick-noodle tsukemen on house-milled Hokkaido wheat finished with yuzu-scented dashi rice.

places.name: 中華そば 双鳩 (Chuka Soba Soukyu)
places.neighborhood: Mibu, Nakagyō-ku (Shijō-Ōmiya)
places.cuisine: Chuka-soba (Chinese-style noodles)

noodles.notes: Medium-thin straight noodles with a crisp bite and pronounced wheat flavor, chosen to bind tightly with the clear shoyu broth in the old-school chuka soba idiom.

ramen.signature_bowl: Chuka soba (中華そば) — a nostalgic chicken-and-pork-bone soy sauce bowl accented with ginger; upgrade to the chashu-men for a generous layer of pork.
ramen.chashu: Braised pork belly (nibuta) — tender, fatty rolls of bara cut, sliced over the bowl in the classic Showa style.
notable_toppings: spicy miso condiment on the side

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui noodles plus a wheat-based shoyu tare; no rice- or konjac-noodle or gluten-free option is documented. Not celiac-safe.

vegan.note: Broth is built on chicken and pork bones with a shoyu tare, and the bowl is dressed with pork belly and back-fat; no plant-based broth or topping option is documented.

ramen.pantheon: A loving revival of a beloved neighborhood chuka soba that once stood on this Mibu corner, the bowl pours a clear chicken-and-pork shoyu broth brightened by ginger and rounded with a gentle melt of pork back-fat — the unmistakable Kyoto soul of light-yet-savory se-abura shoyu. It tastes like the everyday Showa-era ramen that locals built their afternoons around, simple and quietly addictive.

places.name: ラーメン 霽レ空 (Ramen Haresora)
places.neighborhood: Nakagyō-ku, Nijō
places.cuisine: Chuka-soba / negi (green onion) ramen

noodles.notes: Medium-thin noodles. The chuka soba uses flat, rectangular-cut noodles that give a pleasant tongue-feel and clean bite; the negi ramen uses medium-thin straight noodles that the thick, viscous pork-shoyu broth clings to well.

ramen.signature_bowl: Negi Ramen — a rich pork-bone-and-chicken shoyu bowl crowned with a mound of seasoned shiraga-negi (fine white-scallion threads); for a lighter classic, the chuka soba is a clear chicken-and-soy bowl.
ramen.chashu: Thin-sliced braised pork belly on the Negi Ramen; the chuka soba carries three thin slices of conventional braised chashu.

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui ramen noodles and a soy-based (wheat) shoyu tare run through every bowl; no rice- or konjac-noodle or GF-tare option is documented. Not celiac-safe.

vegan.note: Broths are built on chicken bones plus seafood/dried-fish dashi, with pork-back-fat and braised-pork toppings throughout. No documented plant-only (kombu/shiitake/veg) bowl.

ramen.pantheon: A Nijo neighborhood shop with two souls in one room: a clear, nostalgic chicken-and-soy chuka soba in the gentle Kyoto-meets-Tokyo tradition, and a richer pork-bone shoyu Negi Ramen finished with a snowfall of seasoned white-scallion threads and a slick of back-fat that nods to Kyoto's love of se-abura shoyu. You taste the kitchen's careful, additive-light hand in the balance of soy depth and clean stock.

closed.note: Tabelog https://tabelog.com/en/kyoto/A2601/A260203/26027734/ carries the "Closed" badge ("This restaurant is permanently closed."); independently, Google Places lists 「ラーメン 霽レ空 HARESORA」 as CLOSED_PERMANENTLY.

places.name: 担担 四条本店 (Tantan Shijo Honten)
places.neighborhood: Mibu, Nakagyō-ku / Shijō-Ōmiya–Saiin area
places.cuisine: Dandanmen specialist

noodles.notes: Thin-gauge noodles with springy elasticity that grip the thick sesame broth well; a thick-noodle (futomen) substitution is offered.

ramen.signature_bowl: Chashu tantanmen — the creamy sesame tantanmen, optionally dressed up with chashu; a cold (hiyashi) version appears in summer.
ramen.chashu: Braised pork chashu offered as an add-on; the bowl's protein heart is its seasoned ground pork (niku-miso style) stirred into the broth.

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui ramen noodles plus a sesame-paste tantan base built on Chinese seasonings; no rice/konjac noodle or gluten-free option is documented. Not celiac-safe.

vegan.note: Sesame-cream broth carries an animal (chicken/pork) backbone and the bowl is finished with seasoned ground pork; no documented plant-only broth. Not vegan.

ramen.pantheon: A Kyoto take on tantanmen that prizes a deeply creamy, sesame-rich umami over fire — built by a chef out of the Cantonese kitchen, so the soup drinks more like a refined Chinese broth than a chili-oil gut-punch. Heat is left to the diner via table condiments, letting the nutty sesame and savory ground pork carry the soul of the bowl.

places.name: 京都らーめん おおの (Kyoto Ramen Ono)
places.neighborhood: Saiin, Ukyō-ku (within walking distance of Hankyū Saiin Stn)
places.cuisine: Kyoto-style ramen

noodles.notes: Thin, firm noodles that soak up the sharp, dark shoyu broth so the seasoning lands just right; served kime (on the firmer side).

ramen.signature_bowl: Oono Ramen (おおのラーメン) — the sharp, dark-shoyu version crowned with melted back-fat (se-abura) and a heap of green scallions; the milder 京都ラーメン is the gentler sibling of the same broth.
ramen.chashu: Tender braised/roasted pork (焼豚), soft sliced loin/belly that yields into the fatty broth.

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui noodles plus a wheat-based shoyu tare; no rice or konjac noodle alternative is documented. Not celiac-safe.

vegan.note: The broth is built on chicken and pork bones, finished with pork back-fat and pork chashu — no plant-based bowl is offered.

ramen.pantheon: This is Kyoto's hometown soul-food: the se-abura chaccha-kei bowl where a cloudy chicken-and-pork broth is hit with a sharp, sweet-free dark shoyu and blanketed in melted back-fat. You taste the old Kyoto lineage in that punchy-yet-mellow soup — rich and fatty up front, the shoyu cutting clean behind it, the way the city's ramen has tasted for generations.

places.name: らー麺創房 ぱこ (Ramen Soubou Pako)
places.neighborhood: Saiin, Ukyō-ku (around Hankyū Nishikyōgoku Stn)
places.cuisine: Ramen

noodles.notes: Straight medium-width noodles in the signature shio bowl; thinner, firmer noodles paired with the niboshi-forward chuka soba to stand up to the punchy broth. No documentation that noodles are made in-house.

ramen.signature_bowl: Gokujo Shio Ramen (premium salt ramen) — a clear chicken-and-fish broth seasoned with shio tare; the niboshi-forward Cho-Niboshi Chuka Soba is the other pillar, and a shio tsukemen rounds out the lineup.
ramen.chashu: Thinly sliced braised roast pork (four to five slices), moist and tender with a deep, well-developed flavor.

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui ramen noodles plus a shoyu-component tare; no rice or konjac noodle option is documented. Not celiac-safe.

vegan.note: Broth is built on chicken and niboshi/seafood dashi with pork chashu and chicken fat throughout; no plant-only bowl is documented.

ramen.pantheon: This Saiin shop chases clarity over fat: a limpid Kyoto-red-chicken and dried-sardine broth tuned bright with a delicate shio tare, the kind of restrained, dashi-driven bowl that lets the niboshi's umami sing. Its alter ego, a punchy niboshi chuka soba, pushes that dried-fish lineage to the front with an aroma that hits before the first slurp.

places.name: さいラーメン (Sai Ramen)
places.neighborhood: Mibu, Nakagyō-ku (around Nishioji-Sanjō / Sanjō-Ōmae)
places.cuisine: Ramen

noodles.notes: Straight medium-thin noodles from a local Kyoto noodle maker, with a smooth surface and a firm, slightly snappy bite that holds up in the thick broth; regulars suggest ordering them on the firmer side.

ramen.signature_bowl: Wagyu-suji ramen — the thick chicken-and-pork paitan crowned with slow-braised wagyu beef tendon and a sweet Korean-style chili-and-sesame soy accent; the plain ramen and the karaage-and-rice set are the other ways regulars work the bowl.
ramen.chashu: Thick-cut, fall-apart braised pork chashu (some bowls served lightly seared/aburi for an aromatic char), paired with the shop's signature slow-stewed pork cartilage (nankotsu) so tender it needs no chewing — a soki-soba-like touch.
notable_toppings: karaage and rice on the set
free spicy chive oil at the counter

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui ramen noodles and a soy-based tare; the broth is built on long-simmered chicken and pork bones. No rice- or konjac-noodle or gluten-free option is documented.

vegan.note: The soul of the bowl is a heavy chicken-and-pork bone paitan, dressed with pork chashu, cartilage and beef tendon. No plant-based broth is offered.

ramen.pantheon: A thick, collagen-rich chicken-and-pork paitan carrying the DNA of Ichijoji's famed Takayasu, where the chef spent fifteen years at the stockpot — you taste that lineage in the pottari, almost gravy-like sweetness of the soup. This is Kyoto's heavyweight, modern kotteri tori-tonkotsu rather than the city's older thin se-abura shoyu, pushed even richer with a deeper animal punch than the parent shop.

places.name: ラーメン たぬき屋 (Ramen Tanukiya)
places.neighborhood: Fushimi-Momoyama / Chūshojima area (near Fukakusa and Fushimi Stns)
places.cuisine: Chuka-soba / aged tonkotsu / mazesoba

noodles.notes: Noodles from the renowned Kyoto maker Menya Teigaku (麺屋棣鄂). The aged-tonkotsu bowl uses a medium-thick straight noodle with a firm, substantial bite to stand up to the thick broth; the lighter chuka-soba uses a thinner straight cut with a pleasant wheat aroma and crisp snap.

ramen.signature_bowl: Jukusei Tonkotsu Ramen (aged pork-bone ramen) — the kitchen's limited specialty, capped at about 20 bowls each at lunch and dinner. Go DX for extra chashu and a half ajitama, and consider the house "tanuki" meat-miso or keema-style curry topping stirred in.
ramen.chashu: Thick, roughly hand-cut chunks of braised pork belly rather than thin slices — soft and crumbly with fatty seams that melt into a sweet pork-fat richness, glazed in a soy-based tare. The lighter chuka-soba instead gets a tender, well-seasoned chicken chashu.

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui noodles from a Kyoto noodle maker plus a soy-based (wheat) tare run through every bowl; no rice- or konjac-noodle or gluten-free option is documented.

vegan.note: The soul of the menu is long-simmered pork-bone and chicken broth with pork-belly and chicken chashu; no plant-based broth or vegan bowl is documented.

ramen.pantheon: A modern Kyoto crowd-pleaser that refuses one lane: its limited-run star is a creamy, potage-thick pork-bone soup, simmered hard then rested a full day so the umami deepens without any barnyard funk, finished with a forward hit of garlic that rises through the nose on the first sip. Alongside it the kitchen runs a clean, almost nostalgic chicken-shoyu chuka-soba and a much-loved mazesoba, so one counter quietly covers light-and-clear to rich-and-rib-sticking.

places.name: 拉麺 へんてこ (Ramen Henteko)
places.neighborhood: 深草・墨染 (Fukakusa / Sumizome), Fushimi Ward
places.cuisine: Jiro-style / rich tonkotsu / chicken paitan ramen

noodles.notes: Medium / medium-thin noodles with a chewy, springy bite that lets the wheat flavor read through; sources differ on whether they run straight or gently wavy. Cooked a touch firmer for takeout orders.

ramen.signature_bowl: Henteko Shoyu (へんてこ醤油) — the chicken-paitan shoyu bowl. Variants worth knowing: the niboshi-charged "煮干しへんてこッ" and the seafood "魚介へんてこッ."
ramen.chashu: Sources differ: some describe thick chicken chashu blanched shabu-style to shed excess fat while keeping a juicy bite; others describe house slow-braised pork belly, served three generous slices. Either way it's a soft, fatty, melt-leaning cut rather than a lean loin.
notable_toppings: playful fish-shaped snack crackers (おっとっと) on the seafood bowl

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui ramen noodles plus a wheat-based shoyu tare; no rice-noodle, konjac, or gluten-free option is documented. Not celiac-safe.

vegan.note: The broth is built on long-simmered chicken bones and feet, with chicken fat and meat chashu; no plant-based (kombu/shiitake/veg) bowl is documented.

ramen.pantheon: A tori-paitan house from the Fukakusa-Sumizome backstreets of Fushimi, where chicken feet and bones are boiled hard for hours into a milky, gently rich soup that drinks mellow rather than heavy. Its soul is the playful, research-minded spirit of the shop — a clean chicken-cream base finished with shoyu and bent toward niboshi or seafood riffs, a modern Kyoto original rather than any one regional lineage.

places.name: せんぼんぐらばー館 (Senbon Gurabaa-kan)
places.neighborhood: Nishijin, Senbon-dori (Kamigyo-ku), near Kitano-Hakubaicho
places.cuisine: Machi-chūka (neighborhood Chinese) / Nagasaki champon / sara-udon (crispy fried noodles)

noodles.notes: Distinctive thick yellow Nagasaki-champon noodles with a chewy, springy bite that holds up against the loaded broth and toppings; these are champon noodles (made with a unique alkaline lye water), not standard ramen noodles. The sara-udon by contrast uses hair-thin noodles deep-fried crisp.

ramen.signature_bowl: Nagasaki champon (長崎ちゃんぽん) — a milky, umami-deep bowl piled with stir-fried pork, shrimp, squid, chikuwa, naruto, cabbage, bean sprouts, onion and carrot over thick chewy champon noodles. (The sara-udon, with hair-thin crispy fried noodles under a chicken-stock veg-and-seafood ankake, is the equally famous companion specialty.)

gf.note: Champon and sara-udon noodles are wheat-based, and the stir-fried sauce/broth typically carries soy and seafood; no rice- or konjac-noodle or documented GF option exists here.

vegan.note: The signature champon broth is built on pork and chicken bones plus seafood (shrimp, squid), and the bowl is loaded with pork and seafood; no plant-only broth or vegan bowl is documented.

ramen.pantheon: This is not a ramen shop but a beloved old Nishijin town-Chinese counter whose soul is Nagasaki champon — a Kyushu-born dish where pork-and-chicken bones, the sweetness of stir-fried cabbage and the brine of shrimp and squid melt into one milky, gently salted broth. You taste Nagasaki's port-city Chinese lineage rather than any Kyoto ramen tradition: a single warming bowl that is meal, soup and noodle all at once.

places.name: なるかみ (Narukami)
places.neighborhood: Kamigyō-ku, Senbon-dōri (Kitano-Hakubaichō / near Kitano Tenmangū)
places.cuisine: Kyoto-style ramen

noodles.notes: Thin-to-medium straight noodles that play a supporting role to the soup; sources describe them as crisp and springy, sitting low-to-medium hydration with a clean bite.

ramen.signature_bowl: Se-abura (back-fat) shoyu chuka-soba — the house chicken-bone soy bowl scattered with pork back fat and a peppery hit of ichimi chili. Pair it with the famous ebi-meshi (shrimp rice) on the side.
ramen.chashu: Thick-cut braised pork belly, served a couple of slices to a bowl, with a firm, chewy texture that releases meat umami rather than melting away.

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui ramen noodles plus a wheat-based soy (shoyu) tare; no rice- or konjac-noodle or gluten-free tare option is documented. Not celiac-safe.

vegan.note: Chicken-bone broth, pork back-fat oil, and pork-belly chashu are core to every bowl; no plant-based broth or topping option is documented.

ramen.pantheon: A textbook bowl of Kyoto's se-abura shoyu lineage: a chicken-bone soy soup that stays clear and surprisingly light beneath a snowfall of pork back fat, so you taste depth without heaviness. What sets this one apart is the unapologetic dusting of ichimi chili, giving the old-school Kyoto soul a bright, peppery edge.

places.name: みその橋サカイ (Misonobashi Sakai)
places.neighborhood: Kita-ku, Misonobashi (west end of Misono Bridge; toward Kitaōji / Kamigamo Shrine)
places.cuisine: Machi-chūka (neighborhood Chinese) / reimen (cold noodles)

noodles.notes: Medium-thick straight noodles in the traditional Kyoto machi-chuka mold; the broth clings to them. (The shop's signature cold-noodle dish uses far thicker, chewy, glossy egg noodles, but the hot chuka-soba runs medium straight.)

ramen.signature_bowl: The house is famous for its year-round cold noodles (reimen), but the hot bowl to order is the chuka-soba — a Kyoto-style pork-bone-and-chicken shoyu ramen; chashu-men adds extra roast pork.
ramen.chashu: Sliced braised/roast pork (yakibuta) in the old-school machi-chuka manner; the same roast pork that crowns the celebrated cold noodles.

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui noodles plus a soy-sauce (wheat) tare; the cold-noodle sauce also contains soy and egg. No rice or konjac noodle option is documented. Not celiac-safe.

vegan.note: Broth is built on pork-bone and chicken stock and the bowls are dressed with roast pork; the cold-noodle sauce likewise lists chicken extract, pork extract and egg. No documented plant-based broth.

ramen.pantheon: A beloved old-guard Kyoto neighborhood Chinese kitchen near Misonobashi whose hot chuka-soba speaks pure Kyoto lineage — a clear, soy-tinged soup drawn from pork bones and chicken that coats medium-thin straight noodles. Its true legend, though, is the secret-recipe cold noodle eaten all year, a chilled bowl found nowhere else in the same form.

places.name: 一番星 (Ichibanboshi)
places.neighborhood: Sakyō-ku, Okazaki-Kitagoshō-chō (northeast of Heian Shrine)
places.cuisine: Kyoto-style ramen

noodles.notes: Thin, straight noodles with a slightly soft, gentle bite that cling to and soak up the soy-pork broth.

ramen.signature_bowl: Chuka soba (中華そば) — the one bowl this shop makes: a pork-bone-and-chicken soy broth over thin straight noodles, served with a side of house pickles.
ramen.chashu: Braised pork chashu, rested a full day until tender and juicy, with clearly defined lean and fat layers; the fat carries a subtle sweetness.

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui noodles plus a soy-sauce tare made with wheat; no rice-noodle or gluten-free option exists here.

vegan.note: The soul of the bowl is a pork-bone and chicken broth with a touch of pork fat, finished with chashu — no plant-based broth is offered.

ramen.pantheon: A nostalgic survivor of old Kyoto's noodle tradition: pork bones and chicken simmered with onion into a soy-darkened soup that drinks light and mellow yet leaves a faint clinging richness on the lips. It is the gentle, everyday face of Kyoto ramen — pork-bone soy with a whisper of fat rather than the heavy back-fat curtain of the city's louder shops.

places.name: 慈永 (Jiei)
places.neighborhood: Sakyō-ku, Mototanaka
places.cuisine: Kyoto-style ramen

noodles.notes: Chuhoso (medium-thin) straight noodles with a clean, crisp bite and clear wheat character; described as silky and supple, gripping the tea-colored broth well.

ramen.signature_bowl: Chashu Ramen — the standard ramen (around 750 yen) topped with extra slices of the tender pork belly chashu.
ramen.chashu: Long, thin slices of braised pork belly, simmered until they crumble apart at the touch of chopsticks; tender and full-flavored without being heavy.
notable_toppings: thick-cut crunchy menma with a gentle sweetness

gf.note: Standard wheat-and-kansui ramen noodles and a soy-based (wheat) tare; no rice- or konjac-noodle or gluten-free tare option is documented. Not celiac-safe.

vegan.note: Broth is built on chicken and pork bones with a soy tare, finished with pork back fat and topped with pork belly chashu; no plant-based broth or topping option is documented.

ramen.pantheon: A nostalgic bowl in the classic Kyoto se-abura shoyu tradition: a tea-colored broth of chicken and pork bones seasoned with dark soy and floated with a thin veil of pork back fat, so you taste the old-school Kyoto lineage (a Takaraya-style soul carried over from the owner's years at a veteran Kyoto ramen-ya) in every mellow, deep-umami sip. It is the comforting, lived-in Kyoto shoyu — rich and well-developed but never cloying — that defines the city's everyday ramen culture.

places.name: 昆布と麺 喜一 (Konbu to Men Kiichi)
places.neighborhood: 上京区・西五辻東町 (Kitano-Hakubaicho / Kitano Tenmangu area)
places.cuisine: Kombu-specialist ramen and tsukemen

noodles.notes: Whole-grain (zenryūfun) noodles made in-house/for the shop by ramen maker Tōhichi using first-grade Hokkaido Haruyokoi wheat. The bowl (ramen) uses a medium straight whole-grain noodle; the seasonal gagome-kombu tsukemen pairs a thicker, chewier whole-grain noodle chilled in cold water for firm, elastic bite.

ramen.signature_bowl: 昆布らぁめん (Kombu ramen) — a clear shio bowl built entirely on kombu and seafood dashi, topped with the shop's hand-shaved oboro kombu. In warmer months (roughly May–October) the kitchen switches to the がごめ昆布つけ麺 (gagome-kombu tsukemen), with a sticky kombu-rich dip and thick whole-grain noodles.
ramen.chashu: For the ramen, the "chashu" is domestic young chicken breast gently cooked in kombu dashi and salt — lean, delicate, and in keeping with the no-meat-in-the-broth philosophy. The seasonal tsukemen instead uses soft, tender braised pork (nibuta).
notable_toppings: Hand-shaved oboro kombu (true kombu, shaved to order)

gf.note: Noodles are wheat-based whole-grain (Haruyokoi) men with kansui, and the tsukemen dip adds shoyu — both contain wheat/gluten, so not celiac-safe. No documented rice or konjac noodle option.

vegan.note: The broth is uniquely meat-free and additive-free, built on three kombu varieties plus seafood (bonito, dried squid, shellfish). The kombu dashi base itself is plant-derived, but the soup includes katsuo/seafood and the toppings include chicken or pork, so as served it is not vegan. A kombu-and-vegetable-only bowl is not advertised — worth asking, but do not assume.

ramen.pantheon: A one-of-a-kind bowl from a 150-year-old Kyoto kombu house: the soup is pure kelp-and-sea umami — true, Rausu, and Rishiri kombu cold-steeped in soft water, layered with bonito, dried squid and shellfish, and seasoned with nothing but salt. There is no meat and no kaeshi in the pot, so what you taste is the clean, glutamate-rich lineage of dashi itself, finished with kombu shaved over the bowl by hand.

places.name: 稲穂食堂 (Inaho Shokudo)
places.neighborhood: Ichijoji, Sakyo-ku (near Ichijoji Station, Eizan Railway)
places.cuisine: Asian "no-borders"

places.name: コムギノキラメキ〈小麦〉 (Komugi no Kirameki (Komugi))
places.neighborhood: Nishikyo Ward, Kamikatsura Stn (Kamikatsura Maeda-cho)
places.cuisine: Tori-paitan

noodles.notes: House-made noodles from the shop's glass-walled noodle workshop using 100% Hokkaido wheat. The standard paitan bowls use a smooth, chewy (tsuru-mochi) medium-thin straight noodle that suits the delicate-yet-rich soup. The Jiro-style mazesoba 'Komugi no Chikara' instead uses an ultra-thick (3mm, #10 cutter) square straight noodle with strong bite.

ramen.signature_bowl: Shio no Kirameki (salt tori-paitan) — the cleanest expression of the rich, creamy chicken-paitan soup; the soy (Shoyu no Kirameki) and miso versions share the same broth. The shop-exclusive Jiro-style mazesoba "Komugi no Chikara" is the brothless counterpart for big-noodle, back-fat cravings.
ramen.chashu: Seared chicken-thigh chashu — thick, tender slices of thigh meat with a lightly torched/seared surface, served on the paitan bowls. (The Jiro-style Komugi no Chikara mazesoba instead tops with tender pork and back-fat.)

gf.note: Noodles are house-made 100% Hokkaido wheat with kansui and the soy/miso tare contain wheat; no rice or konjac noodle option is documented. Not celiac-safe.

vegan.note: The soul of every bowl is a long-simmered chicken-bone paitan, with chicken or pork chashu and animal-based tare/oil. No plant-broth bowl is offered.

ramen.pantheon: A modern tori-paitan specialist whose soul is a long-simmered chicken broth boiled until it turns milky, creamy and clinging — the cloudy, emulsified style that defines contemporary chicken-paitan ramen rather than any old regional lineage. You taste that pure poultry richness most clearly in the restrained salt (shio) bowl, where the velvety soup, not the seasoning, carries the bowl.

places.name: ラーメン ビスカ (Ramen Viska)
places.neighborhood: Ichijoji / Takano, Sakyo-ku
places.cuisine: Ramen

noodles.notes: House offers a choice of thick or thin noodles. The default with the kotteri is a medium-thick, fairly straight noodle that clings well to the heavy broth; the thick option has a wavy, hand-cut-feeling, springy-chewy texture. Thin noodle also available.

ramen.signature_bowl: Kotteri pork-bone ramen — the ultra-thick emulsified tonkotsu the shop is built on. A clear assari version, an urume-sardine tsukemen, and a Jiro-style "Bis-ro" (mashimashi) are the alternates.
ramen.chashu: Lean, red-meat-forward pork chashu cooked more like a roast than a fatty braise, so it drinks up the heavy broth rather than melting into it.
notable_toppings: harissa chili paste at the table

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui ramen noodles plus a shoyu (wheat) tare and a pork-bone broth; nothing rice- or konjac-based is documented. Not celiac-safe.

vegan.note: Built entirely on a long-simmered pork-bone broth with pork chashu and a shoyu tare; no plant-based bowl exists here.

ramen.pantheon: A modern Kyoto kotteri specialist in the Ichijoji ramen battleground, this bowl chases pure pork-bone density — a broth simmered so far down it turns velvety and potage-thick, the kind a spoon nearly stands up in, all umami and no gaminess. It is a contemporary tonkotsu original rather than a regional copy, with a clear assari counterpart and a North-African harissa kicker that signals the kitchen's playful streak.

places.name: 煌力 (Goriki)
places.neighborhood: Nakagyō-ku / Karasuma-Oike Stn (Nishinotōin-dōri, just south of Anekōji)
places.cuisine: Tantanmen

noodles.notes: Semi-translucent high-hydration thin noodles sourced from a renowned Kyoto noodle maker (Menya Teikaku); springy, snappy 'puri-puri' bite that stands up to the thick sesame soup.

ramen.signature_bowl: THE 担々麺 (THE Tantanmen) — the house standard: a thick, smooth sesame-and-nut soup with freshly ground sesame and house-made chili oil, finished with fragrant Kyoto sansho. Order the tsuke-tantanmen version (served over a tabletop IH burner that keeps the dipping soup hot) for the shop's playful twist, and add the lunch rice set to finish the leftover soup as a stone-baked bibimbap-style kuppa.
ramen.chashu: No sliced chashu — the protein is a spicy miso-seasoned minced-pork soboro stirred into the soup.

gf.note: Wheat noodles with kansui and a sesame/soy-based tantan tare make this unsafe for celiacs; no rice- or konjac-noodle option is documented.

vegan.note: The soup is built on animal stock and the bowl is topped with minced pork; no documented plant-broth, meat-free version.

ramen.pantheon: A modern Kyoto tantanmen specialist where the soul is the soup: a deep, velvety river of freshly ground sesame and nuts riding a savory meat stock, balanced across umami, sweetness, salt and a gentle chili heat. What sets it apart is the bright, fruity numbing perfume of Kyoto sansho instead of dried Sichuan pepper — a distinctly local, aromatic take on the genre.

places.name: まる担 おがわ (Marutan Ogawa)
places.neighborhood: Katsura / Kashihara (Nishikyo-ku) — a residential street nea
places.cuisine: Tantanmen

noodles.notes: Thin, firm straight noodles supplied by the Teigaku noodle maker; they hold up against the rich, chili-oil-forward broth and tangle well with the minced-pork niku-miso. Some reviewers note a slight curl. Kaedama (noodle refills) are popular.

ramen.signature_bowl: Tantanmen (担々麺) at spice level 1 — the house standard. The umami-spicy soup is built on a fragrant, slightly bitter house-made chili oil with rich koku, dressed with niku-miso (minced pork), pak choi, bean sprouts and menma. A miso tantanmen and a vinegar-sharp sanratan (hot-and-sour) version are the main alternatives; wonton and seasonal chilled bowls also appear.
ramen.chashu: No sliced chashu — the meat is niku-miso, a savory minced-pork miso crumble spooned over the noodles in place of a chashu slice.

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui ramen noodles plus a miso/soy-leaning tare and minced-pork niku-miso; no rice-noodle or gluten-free option is documented. Not celiac-safe.

vegan.note: The build centers on a minced-pork niku-miso and a meat/dashi-based broth; no plant-only (kombu/shiitake, no katsuo/pork) bowl is documented. Spice level is adjustable, but the soup and topping are animal-based.

ramen.pantheon: A yatai-style tantanmen worked out of a residential Nishikyo driveway, this is a Japanese-tuned dandan bowl whose soul is its house-made chili oil — fragrant, faintly bitter and built for koku rather than searing heat. With adjustable spice and a savory minced-pork niku-miso over pak choi and sprouts, it sits in the everyday, addictive-comfort lane of Japanese tantanmen rather than the numbing Sichuan or shiru-nashi schools.

places.cuisine: Chicken paitan ramen

noodles.notes: Signature low-temperature aged thin noodles (低温熟成細麺), developed in-house over years. Described as mochi-mochi/springy yet smooth (もちっとプリっとした歯切れの良い食感), they coat well with the emulsified Gion chicken broth. Larger portion (omori) available.

ramen.signature_bowl: Miyako Ramen (みやこらぁ～めん) — the house chicken-paitan bowl, the "Gion white broth" topped with ajitama, scallion, and menma. Gion-honten exclusive: the white-miso version blending Kyoto's traditional Saikyo white miso into the chicken paitan; an extra-rich kotteri (特濃こってり) option is also offered.
ramen.chashu: Long-braised pork chashu cut thick, chosen for a good balance of fat and lean; sweetly seasoned, very tender and meltingly soft in the mouth.

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui ramen noodles plus a shoyu/miso tare make this unsafe for celiacs; no rice- or konjac-noodle or gluten-free tare option is documented.

vegan.note: The soul of every bowl is a long-simmered chicken broth finished with pork back-fat and pork chashu; no plant-based (kombu/shiitake/vegetable) broth bowl is documented.

ramen.pantheon: A modern Kyoto take on tori-paitan: a creamy, emulsified chicken broth — the shop's "Gion white broth" — built on chicken and plenty of vegetables, then lifted with a touch of pork back-fat so it stays deep yet drinkable rather than heavy. It nods to Kyoto's love of rich, fatty soup while threading its own house identity, even folding the city's traditional Saikyo white miso into a signature variant.

places.name: ラーメン 麺対軒 (Ramen Mentaiken)
places.neighborhood: 下京区 (Shijo-Horikawa / near Omiya Station)
places.cuisine: Machi-chūka (neighborhood Chinese) / ramen

noodles.notes: Medium-thick round noodles with a soft, tender surface rather than firm and chewy; the jet-black broth clings to and fully coats them. The noodles play a supporting role to the soup.

ramen.signature_bowl: Shoyu ramen (醤油ラーメン) — a lacquer-black soy bowl — best taken as the famous set with the matching jet-black fried rice (yakimeshi). The clear shio ginger ramen (生姜ラーメン) is the standout alternative.
ramen.chashu: Thin slices of lean braised pork loin, minimal fat — modest, old-school town-Chinese style rather than a thick fatty centerpiece.

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui ramen noodles and a wheat-based dark soy tare; no rice-noodle, konjac, or gluten-free options are documented. Not celiac-safe.

vegan.note: Broth is built on chicken and pork bones with pork chashu and a meat-forward soy tare; no plant-based broth bowl is offered. A vegetable ramen exists on the menu but sits in the same animal broth.

ramen.pantheon: A 1975-founded neighborhood town-Chinese counter pouring Kyoto's signature lacquer-black shoyu ramen — the Shinpuku-lineage bowl whose soup looks like ink yet drinks gentle, the dark soy hitting first before a quiet chicken-and-pork-bone umami rises underneath. The same broth tints the legendary black fried rice that turns this into one of Kyoto's classic ramen-plus-meshi sets.

places.name: らーめん杉千代 (Ramen Sugichiyo)

noodles.notes: Low-hydration thin straight noodles with a chewy, mochi-like bite that holds up against the clinging back-fat broth.

ramen.signature_bowl: Chashu-men (the standard ramen topped with extra braised pork belly) — the cloudy back-fat shoyu bowl that built the shop's reputation.
ramen.chashu: Pork belly braised until meltingly tender, collapsing under chopsticks.

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui noodles and a wheat-based soy (shoyu) tare make this bowl unsafe for celiac diners; no rice- or konjac-noodle alternative is offered.

vegan.note: The soul of the bowl is a pork-and-chicken bone broth finished with pork back fat and braised pork belly — no plant-based option exists.

ramen.pantheon: A revived legend of the Kyoto se-abura tradition: a milky, pork-and-chicken bone broth seasoned with soy and dusted with melted back fat, yet drinking far lighter than its opaque white surface suggests. A default scattering of ichimi chili gives the heritage Kyoto bowl a quiet warmth.

noodles.notes: Thin, low-hydration noodles with a slightly crimped/hand-kneaded wave, made by Kyoto noodle-maker Teigaku (棣鄂). They have a clean bite on arrival and soften gracefully as they drink up the chicken broth; good slurp and throat-feel.

ramen.signature_bowl: Tori-shio soba — the clear chicken salt ramen. Order "ミラノの朝陽 (Milano no Asahi)" for the cleaner, lighter version, or "フィレンツェの夕日 (Firenze no Yuhi)" for the deeper, richer koku bowl. Both are the same chicken-shio soul at different intensities.

notable_toppings: house olive sauce condiment (clam, basil, shallot, olive oil, black pepper) for mid-bowl flavor change

gf.note: Wheat-kansui ramen noodles from a noodle-maker; not celiac-safe. No rice or konjac noodle option is documented. The shio tare itself is salt-based, but the noodles rule it out.

vegan.note: Broth is essentially 99% chicken/jidori and chicken-feet stock, and the protein is chicken ham. No plant-only broth bowl is documented.

ramen.pantheon: A Kyoto chicken-shio specialist that breaks from the city's usual se-abura shoyu lineage: the soul here is a painstaking clear jidori-and-chicken-feet broth, collagen-silky yet clean, seasoned by a salt tare its chef honed studying French cuisine (a three-salt blend of white, pink and black). The French-Italian flourishes — chicken-breast ham, a clam-and-basil olive sauce, a knob of butter — make it a refined modern tori-soba rather than any regional classic.

Its soul is the twist of finishing that rich white broth with a Japanese soy-and-umami edge, giving a clean, refined aftertaste that sets it apart from the dense, gravy-thick tori-paitan that made the city famous.

places.name: あんびしゃす花 (Ambitious Hana)

ramen.signature_bowl: Koku-uma noukou tsukemen (rich concentrated dipping noodles) — the thick seafood-and-pork dipping broth served in a hot stone pot kept actively simmering at the table so it never cools, paired with the shop's signature extra-thick noodles. vegan.note: Broth is built on pork/chicken bones and seafood (gyokai) dashi with braised pork chashu; no documented plant-based broth option.

ramen.pantheon: A modern Kyoto tsukemen specialist in the rich tonkotsu-gyokai (pork-and-seafood double-soup) lineage that swept Japan in the 2000s, but with its own signature theatrics: the concentrated dipping broth arrives in a hot stone pot, simmering at your table so the last mouthful is as scorching as the first. places.name: 京一 本店 (Kyoichi Honten)
places.neighborhood: Nakagyō-ku, Shijō-Ōmiya (right by Hankyū Ōmiya Stn)
places.cuisine: Machi-chūka (neighborhood Chinese) / casual eatery (taishū-shokudō)

noodles.notes: Smooth-textured (tsurun) house noodles that slip easily; the curry-chukasoba uses custom-made thinner noodles chosen to cling to the thick curry-an while resisting sogginess.

ramen.signature_bowl: Curry Chukasoba (カレー中華) — house ramen noodles drowned in a thick, dashi-rich Japanese-style curry an, gently spiced and sweetened by braised wagyu beef. The plain Chukasoba (中華そば) is the classic clear-soup alternative.
ramen.chashu: Thin-sliced braised pork-belly chashu (about three pieces) in the standard chukasoba.

ramen.pantheon: A survivor of postwar Kyoto's neighborhood shokudo culture, this is honest machi-chuka 中華そば: a clean, amber chicken-gara soup softened with the kombu-and-katsuo dashi of an udon shop, finished with a gentle shoyu tare. Its famous curry-chukasoba buries those same noodles under a thick, dashi-forward Japanese curry an — comfort food rather than a specialist's bowl.

places.name: 廣東餐館 鳳飛 (Kanton Sankan Houhi)

places.cuisine: Kyoto machi-chūka (Kyoto-style neighborhood Chinese)

ramen.signature_bowl: Karashisoba (からしそば / 撈麺) — thin noodles under a glossy chicken-and-kombu ankake gravy loaded with pork, small shrimp, bamboo shoot and pepper, finished with a sharp lift of Japanese mustard (karashi).
ramen.chashu: The karashisoba carries sliced pork simmered into the gravy rather than a sit-on-top chashu; the gomoku ramen adds yakibuta-style roasted pork slices. No aburi or smoked loin — restrained Kyoto-Chinese pork.

gf.note: Wheat-kansui noodles and a soy-based seasoning; the karashisoba gravy is also thickened with wheat-adjacent starch and built on a shared kitchen — no documented rice/konjac-noodle or GF option.

vegan.note: The broth and gravy are built on chicken bones (with kombu) and the noodle dishes carry pork and shrimp; no documented plant-only bowl.

ramen.pantheon: A direct descendant of the fabled Houmai school of Kyoto town-Chinese, this kitchen speaks in the gentle, dashi-forward dialect of 京中華 — chicken bones quietly married to kombu, almost no garlic, very little surface oil. Its soul is the karashisoba: a clear-souled chicken-kombu lineage thickened into a silky ankake and lit by a clean stripe of yellow mustard, restraint that lets every shrimp, pork slice and bamboo shoot taste of itself.

places.name: なぶら (Nabura)
places.neighborhood: Kamigyō-ku, Kitano-Hakubaichō (toward Kitano Tenmangū / Kamishichiken)
places.cuisine: Mackerel-broth / seafood-based ramen / tsukemen

noodles.notes: Flat, crimped thick noodles (ramen) sourced from an established Kyoto noodle maker; the tsukemen uses a chewy whole-wheat flat noodle. Built to grip the dense saba broth.

ramen.signature_bowl: Saba ramen (鯖ラーメン) — the thick, condensed mackerel-and-kombu broth crowned with saba tatsuta-age
ramen.chashu: No pork chashu; the protein centerpiece is saba tatsuta-age (lightly battered, fried marinated mackerel) set atop the bowl in place of a meat slice.

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui ramen and tsukemen noodles, plus a battered fried-mackerel topping (tatsuta-age uses flour), make this unsafe for celiacs. No rice- or konjac-noodle option is documented.

vegan.note: The entire identity of the bowl is a mackerel (saba) and kombu dashi, and the signature topping is fried fish. Despite using no pork or land-animal stock, it is fundamentally fish-based and not vegan.

ramen.pantheon: A modern Kyoto original built by a 35-year washoku chef: instead of pork or chicken, the soul here is a single fish — saba — simmered with kombu into a dense, potage-thick broth with no chemical seasoning, no fish powder, and no animal stock at all. You taste pure mackerel umami rounded by kelp, a clean-yet-rich bowl that stands apart from Kyoto's usual se-abura shoyu lineage.

places.name: 麺ビストロ Nakano (Men Bistro Nakano)
places.neighborhood: 四条烏丸 (Shijō-Karasuma), 中京区
places.cuisine: French-inspired creative ramen

noodles.notes: Flat, high-hydration wavy noodles with a soft, mochi-like chew that drink up the light broth; pale rather than the usual yellow kansui color. The black-shoyu bowl reads a touch more medium-thick and springy. One source described thin noodles, but most accounts point to flatter medium strands.

ramen.signature_bowl: 白しょうゆ麺 (White Shoyu Men) — a clear, refined French-style chicken-and-seafood broth seasoned with pale white tamari shoyu
ramen.chashu: Light chicken chashu — gentle and low-fat, tuned to sit under the delicate white broth rather than dominate it. The retro black-shoyu bowl instead uses an old-school grilled pork (yakibuta) style.

gf.note: Chinese-style wheat-and-kansui noodles throughout, and the shoyu tare is wheat-based. No rice/konjac noodle or GF-tare option is documented; not celiac-safe.

vegan.note: Broths are built on French chicken fond (fonds de volaille) plus fish/seafood stock and bushi dashi, with chicken or pork chashu. No plant-only (kombu/shiitake/veg) bowl is documented. The seasonal creamy potage noodles still use dairy and a chicken-stock base.

ramen.pantheon: A modern-original Kyoto creation from a French-trained chef who builds his soup like a classical kitchen — a clear chicken fond de volaille married to Japanese bushi dashi, then seasoned with pale white tamari shoyu so the bowl drinks like an elegant consommé rather than a ramen. You taste the French-Japanese lineage in the soup: refined, herb-touched, and a world away from Kyoto's usual back-fat shoyu.

places.name: 真打 英多朗 (Shinuchi Eitaro)
places.neighborhood: Nakagyō-ku, Shijō-Ōmiya
places.cuisine: Yuzu ramen / Sanuki udon

noodles.notes: Straight thin noodles made from domestic wheat with deliberately low kansui content, custom-made by a noodle maker the shop courted for years; clean finish with good grip on the broth.

ramen.signature_bowl: Yuzu Ramen (ゆずラーメン) — a refined chicken-and-bonito shoyu bowl finished with abundant back-fat and a generous squeeze of fresh yuzu.
ramen.chashu: Braised pork shoulder loin (kata-rosu) so tender it crumbles when lifted with chopsticks; sourced from a noted Kyoto butcher.

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui ramen noodles plus a soy-sauce (wheat) tare; this is a noodle house (also serving udon), so no gluten-free option is documented.

vegan.note: Broth is built on chicken bones and bonito first-dashi, with pork back-fat and braised pork chashu throughout; no plant-based broth or topping option is documented.

ramen.pantheon: Born from a veteran udon master's own dashi craft, this bowl marries a seven-hour chicken-bone stock with bonito first-dashi and a soy tare, then lights it up with fresh yuzu — its soul is the Kyoto se-abura shoyu lineage softened and brightened, where sweet pork back-fat and citrus acidity meet over a clear, fragrant soup. It is less a regional copy than a Kyoto original: the depth of a noodle shop's broth wearing a coat of yuzu.

places.name: ラーメン あかつき (Ramen Akatsuki)
places.neighborhood: Sakyō-ku, Kitashirakawa
places.cuisine: Back-fat (seabura) shoyu ramen

noodles.notes: Special-order thin, straight noodles with firm chew (koshi); aged. A slim noodle that carries the back-fat-glossed soup.

ramen.signature_bowl: Chashu ramen (or the loaded "Akatsuki Special") — the standard pork-bone-and-chicken shoyu bowl crowned with extra back-fat and sliced chashu; sizes run from kids/chibi up to jumbo.
ramen.chashu: Tender braised pork laid over the bowl — described as fatty, melt-in-the-mouth slices fanned out like flower petals; sources vary between loin and belly, both braised rather than grilled.

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui noodles in a soy-sauce (wheat) tare over a pork/chicken broth — no gluten-free noodle or tare option is documented. Not celiac-safe.

vegan.note: Soul of the bowl is a pork-bone and chicken broth finished with pork back-fat and braised pork chashu — no plant-based broth or topping option is documented.

ramen.pantheon: A neighborhood institution of Kyoto's signature se-abura shoyu lineage: a pork-bone-and-chicken soy broth, simmered overnight and rested a full day, then glossed with sweet pork back-fat that pools on the surface yet drinks far lighter than its creamy look suggests. The clean koku of that soup over slim straight noodles is the taste of old Kita-Shirakawa.

places.name: 特製ラーメン 大中 本店 (Tokusei Ramen Daichu Honten)
places.neighborhood: Fushimi-ku, Momoyama (right by Kintetsu Momoyama-Goryō-mae Stn, under the Fushimi-Momoyama railway viaduct)
places.cuisine: Tonkotsu-shoyu ramen

noodles.notes: Custom-milled slightly-thin straight noodles (from a local noodle maker) built to resist softening and to grip the heavy broth. Firmness is one of the free customization choices.

ramen.signature_bowl: Daichu Ramen — the rich pork-bone-and-chicken shoyu tonkotsu; the "Tokuno" extra-concentrated version is the move for devoted kotteri fans, with thin straight noodles, a selectable pork cut, and free add-ons (bean sprouts, scallion, egg, kimchi).
ramen.chashu: Braised Kyushu pork with selectable cuts — melt-on-the-tongue belly (bara), shoulder-loin (kata-rosu), and lean loin (rosu); relatively lean, soaking up the sauce-thick broth. Diners can choose or combine cuts.

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui ramen noodles and a soy-sauce (wheat) tare; no rice/konjac noodle or GF-tare option is documented. Not celiac-safe.

vegan.note: Broth is pork bone plus chicken frames simmered 24 hours, with pork chashu and an optional fish-pork variant. No plant-based broth bowl exists here.

ramen.pantheon: A Kyushu-style tonkotsu transplanted to a Fushimi railway underpass: pork bones and chicken frames are cracked in-house and boiled hard for a full day into a white, potage-thick broth so dense a chopstick can stand in it, then seasoned with shoyu for a soy-tonkotsu soul. It drinks rich and clinging yet finishes surprisingly clean — among the most kotteri bowls in all of Kyoto.

places.name: 元祖熟成細麺 香来 壬生本店 (Ganso Jukusei Hosomen Kourai Mibu Honten)
places.neighborhood: Nakagyō-ku, Mibu (Shijō-Ōmiya / toward Nijō Castle)
places.cuisine: Kyoto-style chuka-soba

noodles.notes: The shop's namesake: jukusei hosomen, thin noodles aged about four days for a firm, glossy bite with a clean throat-feel. Other bowls (Korai-men, miso tsukemen) use flat or thick noodles, but the flagship shoyu bowl is built on these aged thin straight noodles.

ramen.signature_bowl: Ramen (the standard chuka-soba): a chicken-and-pork shoyu broth simmered around twelve hours with aromatic vegetables, finished with a scattering of pork back-fat (se-abura chatcha), poured over the house aged thin noodles.
ramen.chashu: Thin-sliced braised pork loin chashu; on the chashu-men it is fanned petal-like around the rim in the old Kyoto presentation, and a richer toro-niku (fatty cut) version is offered as a limited topping.

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui aged noodles plus a wheat-based shoyu tare; no rice or konjac noodle option is documented. Not celiac-safe.

vegan.note: Broth is chicken and pork bone simmered with vegetables, the tare is shoyu, and back-fat and chashu are pervasive. No plant-only bowl is documented.

ramen.pantheon: This is Kyoto's beloved se-abura shoyu lineage in the round, descended from the old Takaraya/Daio school: a deep chicken-and-pork soy soup blanketed with floating pork back-fat for a sweet, clinging richness over an otherwise clear base. The house twist is the aged thin noodle that gives the bowl a brisk, glossy bite where most Kyoto back-fat shops lean heavier and chewier.

places.name: 中華そば笑麺 (Chuka Soba Shomen)
places.neighborhood: Horikawa shopping street / Kamigyō-ku (Horikawa-dōri, Shimodachiuri–Marutamachi; Marutamachi Subway Stn / toward Imadegawa)
places.cuisine: Kyoto-style back-fat (seabura) / machi-chūka (neighborhood Chinese)

noodles.notes: Thin, straight low-hydration noodles built to carry the back-fat-laden aged soy soup; described as a bowl you never tire of even daily.

ramen.signature_bowl: 中華そば (chuka soba) — chicken-bone soy ramen crowned with melted back fat; upgrade to the 笑麺 / chashu-men for extra pork and ajitama.
ramen.chashu: Melt-in-your-mouth braised pork chashu, tender and softly stewed rather than char-grilled.

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui noodles plus a wheat-based aged soy tare; no rice/konjac-noodle or GF-tare option is documented. Not celiac-safe.

vegan.note: Soup is built on chicken bones with pork back fat and braised pork chashu; no plant-based broth is offered.

ramen.pantheon: A textbook bowl of Kyoto's beloved se-abura shoyu lineage: a chicken-bone broth darkened with aged soy sauce and blanketed in glistening, collagen-rich pork back fat. The fat reads rich to the eye yet the soup underneath stays clean and moreish — exactly the kind of nostalgic, never-tiring Kyoto noodle the neighborhood has leaned on since 1993.

places.address_ja: 京都府京都市上京区西堀川通下立売上る四町目55 下立売団地1F

places.name: 麺屋 一麺専心 (Menya Ichimen Senshin)
places.neighborhood: Kamigyō-ku, Senbon-Marutamachi (northwest of Nijō Castle) / ~11 min walk from JR Nijō Stn
places.cuisine: Ramen

noodles.notes: Medium-thick, high-hydration wavy noodles from the Kyoto maker Teigaku (Teikaku); chewy and slurpable, built to drag up and cling to the thick broth, with throat-feel prioritized over bite.

ramen.signature_bowl: Ultra-rich tonkotsu ramen (超濃厚豚骨らーめん) — pork bone and water only, around 1 kg of bone per bowl; the chicken paitan (鶏白湯) is the lighter, collagen-rich second pillar.
ramen.chashu: Tender braised pork belly, richly fatty so the fat melts juicily in the mouth; the tonkotsu bowl is piled generously, with one thick slice plus several thin slices.
notable_toppings: side plate of warm vegetables (cabbage, bean sprouts, carrot, onion) to add as you like

gf.note: Wheat-and-kansui ramen noodles plus a shoyu (wheat) tare; nothing rice- or konjac-noodle based is offered, so this is not celiac-safe.

vegan.note: Every bowl is built on long-simmered pork bone or chicken broth with pork belly chashu and a shoyu tare; no plant-only broth is offered. The complimentary warm vegetable plate is the only animal-free element.

ramen.pantheon: A modern Kyoto bone-broth specialist that does the rare double act of an ultra-thick pork-bone soup — boiled down from roughly a kilo of bone per bowl until it turns gluey and viscous, in the spirit of Kyoto's famously dense kotteri lineage — alongside a smoother, collagen-rich chicken paitan. The pork tonkotsu, not Hakata-thin but heavy and emulsified, is the bowl that defines the shop's soul.

places.name: らーめん 遊貯 (Ramen Yucho)
places.neighborhood: Shimogyō-ku, Shijō-Kawaramachi (near Kyoto-Kawaramachi Stn)
places.cuisine: Kyoto-style ginger-shoyu ramen

places.name: 麺屋 鼎（KANAE） (Menya Kanae)
places.neighborhood: Shijo-Omiya / Mibu (Nakagyo-ku)
places.cuisine: Jiro-style ramen

noodles.notes: Thick, wide, curly Jiro-style noodles from the Teian maker, made specifically for jiro-kei — chewy with good elasticity, built to drag up fat and seasoning. Said to be relatively approachable for Jiro beginners.

ramen.signature_bowl: KANAE no Jiro (鼎の二郎) — a Jiro-style bowl piled with yasai (bean sprouts, some cabbage), pork and abura, finished with premium wagyu (Kobe/Omi) beef fat. Choose shio or shoyu and soup or no-soup (mazesoba) at the ticket machine; call your garlic/yasai/abura. Shio is the quieter, fat-forward recommendation.
ramen.chashu: Thick-cut braised pork slices in the standard bowl (two pieces); the shop also leans into beef, with long-simmered gelatinous beef achilles featured as a signature protein in some bowls.

gf.note: Jiro-style wheat-and-kansui noodles plus shoyu/shio tare and a pork-and-beef fat broth — no documented rice or konjac noodle, not celiac-safe.

vegan.note: Built on pork tonkotsu with rendered wagyu beef fat, pork chashu and beef achilles — no plant-based broth option documented.

ramen.pantheon: A Kyoto take on the Tokyo-born Jiro lineage — the mountain of bean sprouts, garlic and glistening fat is pure jiro-kei — but the soul here is the swap of ordinary pork back-fat for premium wagyu (Kobe/Omi) beef fat, which lends the rich tonkotsu base a sweeter, more elegant, less leaden finish. You taste that beefy refinement riding over the usual Jiro stomp.
